sec: Gonadotropin and GH deficits, masked DI and pituitary apoplexy

items.q: Match the gender to the clinical manifestation of gonadotropin (FSH/LH) deficiency — 1) Males 2) Females … A) Loss of energy, loss of libido, and bone/muscle wasting B) Menstrual irregularity, hot flushes, dry skin, and irritability
items.exp: Males experience loss of libido and muscle/bone wasting; females experience cycle irregularities, hot flushes, and dry skin. (Book p953)

items.q: Which constellation of features characterizes growth hormone deficiency in adults?
opts: Central obesity, hypertriglyceridemia, endothelial dysfunction, and reduced lean body mass
Linear dwarfism, delayed fontanelle closure, and micropenis
Severe hypercalcemia, nephrolithiasis, and cutaneous calcinosis
Generalized lipoatrophy with hepatic steatosis and ketoacidosis
items.exp: Adult GH deficiency features central obesity, hypertriglyceridemia, endothelial dysfunction, reduced lean mass, and psychosocial issues. (Book p953)

items.q: A 40-year-old male with craniopharyngioma and panhypopituitarism has normal daily urine volume. Following initiation of hydrocortisone and levothyroxine replacement, he develops severe polyuria and thirst. What explains this phenomenon?
opts: Glucocorticoid deficiency previously masked diabetes insipidus by impairing free water clearance
Levothyroxine exerted immediate osmotic diuresis on proximal renal tubules
Hydrocortisone directly blocked V2 vasopressin receptors in collecting ducts
Pituitary stalk manipulation during examination provoked transient neurogenic shock
items.exp: Diabetes insipidus in hypopituitarism is masked by adrenal/thyroid insufficiency impairing free water clearance; hormone replacement unmasks the polyuria. (Book p953)

items.q: Assess the clinical severity of secondary hypopituitarism: I Secondary hypopituitarism and secondary adrenal insufficiency are generally less severe than primary failure. II Initiating thyroxine in untreated hypocortisolemia can precipitate an acute adrenal crisis.
opts: Both I and II are true
Both I and II are false
items.exp: Secondary hypopituitarism is less severe due to preserved aldosterone; thyroxine accelerates cortisol clearance, worsening hypocortisolemia. (Book p953)

items.q: Which sign is classically ABSENT in secondary hypopituitarism compared to primary glandular failure?
items.exp: Secondary hypopituitarism lacks myxedema/periorbital effusion and hyperpigmentation; hypoglycemia and fatigue are present. (Book p953)

items.q: Pituitary apoplexy is defined pathophysiologically as:
opts: Acute intra-pituitary hemorrhage or infarction within the sella
Autoimmune lymphocytic infiltration of the infundibular stalk
Congenital cystic herniation through the diaphragma sellae
Pyogenic bacterial abscess of the sphenoid sinus
items.exp: Pituitary apoplexy is an acute emergency caused by intra-pituitary hemorrhage or infarction. (Book p953)

items.q: The most common predisposing etiology underlying acute pituitary apoplexy is a pre-existing pituitary ___.
items.exp: A pituitary mass (adenoma) is the most common cause of pituitary apoplexy. (Book p953)

items.q: A 48-year-old male presents with sudden progressive retro-orbital headache over 1 to 2 days, accompanied by complete left third-nerve ophthalmoplegia with ptosis, hypotension, and blood glucose of 52 mg/dL. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.exp: Pituitary apoplexy presents with progressive headache (1-2 days), meningism, ophthalmoplegia/ptosis, hypotension, and hypoglycemia. (Book p953)

items.q: Match the clinical manifestation of pituitary apoplexy to its underlying mechanism — 1) Progressive severe headache 2) Ptosis and diplopia 3) Acute hypotension and hypoglycemia … A) Acute intra-sellar expansion stretching the diaphragma sellae B) Compression of cranial nerves III, IV, or VI in cavernous sinus C) Sudden acute ACTH deficiency and cortisol collapse
items.exp: Intrasellar expansion causes headache; cavernous nerve compression causes ptosis/ophthalmoplegia; acute ACTH loss causes hypotension/hypoglycemia. (Book p953)

items.q: What spontaneous medical conditions can predispose to pituitary apoplexy in the absence of a diagnosed tumor?
opts: Diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and sickle cell anemia
Rheumatoid arthritis, systemic sclerosis, and lupus
Celiac disease, ulcerative colitis, and hemochromatosis
items.exp: Spontaneous apoplexy can be triggered by diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and sickle cell anemia. (Book p953)

items.q: On cranial MRI, acute intra-sellar hemorrhage in pituitary apoplexy characteristically appears as a ___ signal on T1-weighted sequences.
items.exp: Acute hemorrhage within a pituitary adenoma appears as a hyperintense signal on MRI. (Book p953)

items.q: Which clinical feature is NOT part of the presentation of acute pituitary apoplexy?
opts: Progressive headache developing over 1 to 2 days
items.exp: Pituitary apoplexy causes hypotension and hypoglycemia from acute cortisol collapse, not severe hypertension. (Book p953)
